meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Only Unnatural Sex Act Is That Which One Cannot Perform'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Alfred Kinsey, but never located in anything he wrote. Earliest known printing: a 1963 recollection, seven years after his death. Here is the paper trail.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Kinsey and consistent with the argument his books actually made — but no book, paper, lecture text or recording of his has ever been shown to contain the sentence. The earliest known printing is an August 1963 magazine article in which another man recalls hearing Kinsey say it, seven years after Kinsey’s death, and Quote Investigator has found no direct evidence he wrote or spoke it ↗.

source.excerpt: I remember Dr. Kinsey once said that the only unnatural sex act is that which one cannot perform.
trail: 1779 — a precursor, not a source. In Sheridan’s The Critic ↗, Sneer answers an objection about an implausible plot: “Certainly nothing is unnatural, that is not physically impossible.” The same logical move, a different subject.

August 1963 — the first close match. Harold L. Call, president of the Mattachine Society, writes in the Mattachine Review that he remembers Kinsey saying it. Quote Investigator verified the page against library scans ↗. Kinsey had been dead since 1956.

21 January 1966 — it reaches the mass market. An unsigned Time essay ↗ quotes it as Kinsey’s, in the reworded form “that which you cannot perform.” The New York Times repeats the attribution in November 1967, and quotation dictionaries pick it up from 1979.

2009 to today — still unsourced. Wikiquote listed the line among Kinsey quotes awaiting a reliable source ↗; another line on that list has since been sourced to his 1953 report and promoted. This one has not.
source.excerptNote: These are Call’s words, not Kinsey’s: a recollection of something he says he heard, printed seven years after Kinsey died in 1956. Quote Investigator verified the passage against scans of the August 1963 issue — which establishes that Call wrote it, not that Kinsey said it.

source.rightsNote: The sentence has never been tied to a work by Kinsey, so there is no publication date on which a copyright status could turn — we assert none. author.heading: Alfred Kinsey
author.metaLine: 1894–1956 · American sexologist and biologist · founded the Institute for Sex Research, 1947
author.bio: Alfred Kinsey was an American sexologist, biologist and professor of entomology and zoology who founded the Institute for Sex Research at Indiana University in 1947 — today the Kinsey Institute. He is best known for Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953), the two volumes known as the Kinsey Reports, which made him a household name and a lightning rod. The line on this page fits the reputation those books built for him, which is very likely why it stuck to him — but it has never been found in them.

misattribution.heading: Who else it gets hung on
misattribution.intro: No rival originator has been established, but the sentence has been loose enough for decades to pick up other famous names — and to change wording as it travels. The three modern credits below are all later than the Kinsey attribution, and none is sourced to a text either — the fourth entry is an earlier echo, not a rival origin.

items.scope: “The only unnatural sexual behaviour is none at all”
items.why: A shortened variant was ascribed to Freud in the 1987 Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations ↗. Quote Investigator has not traced that variant to Freud either.

items.scope: “The only unnatural act is one which cannot be performed”
items.why: A 2005 book records the line as Hollander’s email sign–off ↗ — using a saying already forty years in print, not coining it.

items.scope: “The only unnatural act is the one which cannot be performed”
items.why: A 2005 blog collection of slogans transcribed from badges credited this wording to Burroughs ↗, with no work cited.

items.scope: “Certainly nothing is unnatural, that is not physically impossible”
items.why: Sneer says this in Act II of The Critic (1779) ↗ — but he is talking about implausible plots on stage, not sex. It is the same logical move in a different argument, and there is no evidence of a chain connecting it to the modern line.

misattribution.truthLine: What is actually established: the sentence is first recorded in print in August 1963, seven years after Kinsey’s death, as one man’s recollection of hearing him say it — and no work written or spoken by Kinsey has been found to contain it ↗.

context.heading: Why this one stuck
lead: The line works because it performs a magic trick in eleven words: it takes “unnatural,” a moral word, and redefines it as a physical one. Anything a body can do is natural by definition, so the category empties itself. That is very close to the argument Kinsey’s reports were understood to be making — which is precisely why almost nobody stopped to ask whether he said it.

Its documented career runs through respectable rooms fast. It appears in a movement magazine in August 1963, then in an unsigned Time essay of 21 January 1966 ↗ that used it to sum up Kinsey’s position, and by November 1967 in the New York Times, where Webster Schott called the assurance “a conundrum of semantics” ↗. Three citations in four years, and not one of them points to anything Kinsey published.
context.detailsSummary: The wording drift, and the other names it has been hung on
detailsBody: The exact form on this page — that which one cannot perform — is the 1963 wording. The version that went mainstream swaps in the second person: that which you cannot perform, which is what Time printed in 1966 and what quote sites reproduce today. Quote Investigator notes the variation explicitly; neither form has been tied to a text by Kinsey.

Loose lines drift to other famous names, and this one has drifted a lot. A shortened variant has been ascribed to Sigmund Freud, used as an email sign–off by Xaviera Hollander, and printed on buttons under William Burroughs’s name. None of those trails leads anywhere earlier than the Kinsey attribution.
context.pull: Every printed record of Kinsey saying this postdates his death.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest close match known to QI is an August 1963 Mattachine Review article by Harold L. Call (vol. 9 no. 8, start p. 4, quote p. 12) reading “I remember Dr. Kinsey once said that the only unnatural sex act is that which one cannot perform”; QI has not located any direct evidence Kinsey wrote or spoke it; Sheridan’s 1779 The Critic contains the precursor; the 1966 Time and 1967 NYT (Webster Schott, “a conundrum of semantics”) attributions; 1979 Rowes Book of Quotes; 1987 Freud variant; 2005 Hollander and Burroughs credits.

The Time essay “The Homosexual in America,” dated 21 January 1966, contains: “Kinsey had a lot to do with this, for to him all sexual pleasure was equally valid. ‘The only unnatural sex act,’ he said, ‘is that which you cannot perform.’”

Wikiquote’s Talk:Alfred Kinsey page lists “The only unnatural sex act is that which you cannot perform” under an Unsourced heading opened in September 2009, inviting editors to supply a reliable source and move it to the article; another entry in the same list was later marked MOVED once sourced to p. 8 of Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953).

The Wikiquote article Alfred Kinsey contains only sourced quotations, grouped under Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948), Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953) and Abortion in the United States (1958); it gives his dates as 23 June 1894 – 25 August 1956 and does not contain the ‘only unnatural sex act’ line.

The full text of Sheridan’s The Critic contains Sneer’s line “Certainly nothing is unnatural, that is not physically impossible”, immediately after Puff’s speech about a play showing things strange enough that though they never did, they might happen.
An Internet Archive scan of The Critic independently carries the same passage, placing Sneer’s line in Act II, Scene 1.

Alfred Kinsey lived 23 June 1894 – 25 August 1956; he was an American sexologist, biologist and professor of entomology and zoology who founded the Institute for Sex Research at Indiana University in 1947 (now the Kinsey Institute) and wrote Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953).

Harold Leland “Hal” Call (1917–2000) was an American LGBT rights activist who became president of the Mattachine Society after the 1953 resignations of its original leadership, and co-founded the press that printed the Mattachine Review.
